title: Shut a cold-supply ball valve a quarter turn to its stop, leaving the hot one open
instruction: Shut off the cold supply at its blue-gripped ball valve, leaving the red-gripped hot valve open, and let go of it.
context: Shutting off one supply line is a household chore: before a washing machine or laundry tub fill hose, a faucet or a toilet fill valve is changed, or when a hose bursts, someone turns the quarter-turn ball valve on that line, as on a water heater or a house's main shutoff; a plumber does the same before any repair on a live line. Here only the cold line of a laundry tub is shut; the hot line stays in service. The hard parts, in order: (1) pick the valve: the two are identical and 203 mm apart, and only the grip colour says which line it is; (2) get the hand onto the trailing side of a 21 mm round grip, 16 mm over the pipe; (3) push it on the lever's arc through the whole 90 degrees against the valve's friction, with nothing to snap it home: a lever left part way still passes water, and a push off the arc rides up the round grip or slips past it; (4) let go with the lever on its stop. One arm can do this; the task does not claim two.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is z 0 (all heights are above it). x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of their midpoint, z up; arm bases at y +305 mm and -305 mm. The table is the floor of a utility alcove where the hot and cold supply stubs for a laundry tub come out of the wall, built from fixed parts; the alcove is open above and in front. (1) Back panel: 1/2 in (12.7 mm) plywood, x 400 to 412.7 mm, y -438 to +438 mm (flush with the side panels' outer faces), 300 mm high. (2) Two side panels, 18 mm plywood, x 200 to 412.7 mm, 300 mm high, inner faces at y +420 mm and -420 mm. (3) Two 1/2 in copper supply stubs (15.9 mm OD, type L), along x at 70 mm height, from the panel's face to their open ends at x 140 mm; the left stub at y +101.5 mm is the cold supply, the right one at y -101.5 mm the hot supply (8 in, 203 mm, apart). Each has a chrome escutcheon (52 mm across, 4 mm thick) on the panel and two plastic saddle pipe clips, 12 mm wide, on 16 x 30 mm wood standoff posts from the floor, at x 345 mm and x 205 mm. (4) On each stub, stem axis at x 270 mm, a 1/2 in lead-free brass full-port ball valve with solder (sweat) ends, modelled on the Apollo 94ALF-203-01A (about US$11 to 31 at distributors; maker's sheet SS1186: 2.05 in, 52 mm, end to end, 5/8 in sockets for this tube): body 52 mm end to end, 30 mm across (est), a stem rising to a 24 mm chrome stop plate whose top is 94 mm up, with two tabs that stop the lever at 0 and at 90 degrees. (5) On each stem, a flat lever 18 x 6 mm lying 97 mm up (27 mm above the pipe's axis), from 12 mm behind the stem axis to 130 mm in front of it, with a round grip 21 mm across and 60 mm long over its outer end (the grip's middle is 100 mm from the stem); the cold grip is blue, the hot grip red. Lever with grip 50 g. Real lever (the stock handle is 90 mm long and higher, so it is cut down and extended): cut the stock handle off 40 mm from the stem axis, keeping its nut, hub and the valve's own stops at 0 and at 90 degrees; bolt on top of it, with two M4 bolts at 25 and 35 mm from the stem, a 120 mm length of 6061 aluminium flat bar 18 x 6 mm starting 20 mm from the stem, bent down 23 mm (two 45 degree bends) between 40 and 63 mm from the stem, so that from 63 mm out to its tip, 130 mm from the stem axis, its centre line is 97 mm above the table (set with a steel rule from the table top). Grip: blue or red vinyl electrical tape wound over the outer 60 mm to 21 mm round (calipers), its middle 100 mm from the stem. Bar, bolts and tape weigh about 50 g (kitchen scale). Both levers start open: lying along the pipe, pointing at the robot. Seen from above the valve shuts clockwise: the lever swings toward +y, ending across the pipe against the stop at 90 degrees (pointing along +y). Breakaway and run torque are 0.20 N m (est), 2.0 N at the middle of the grip; the lever stays where it is left. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: End state plus the whole run, from the two levers' angles, the frame's pose and both grippers, read every control step (20 Hz); the score is the last step's. A: the cold lever's angle from open, seen from above, clockwise positive (0 along the pipe, 90 against the stop, across it). Score 0 if at any time the hot lever turns more than 10 degrees from open, or the frame (panels, stubs and valve bodies, one fixed part) moves more than 5 mm; both are latched. Hands off: on every step of the last 1 s both grippers' finger zones (the 38 mm from each pad tip back toward the wrist, with the fingers' width) are 30 mm or more from the cold lever and the cold valve body (housing, end sleeves, stem and stop plate). Still: over the last 1 s A changes by under 2 degrees. Score 0 unless hands off and still, and 0 for A above 95 degrees (a failed stop). Otherwise: 1.0 for A from 88 degrees up to the stop at 90 (read up to 95; the stop tab is where the ball's port stands square across the seats, and 2 degrees allow for reading the card); 0.5 for A from 45 up to 88; 0.25 for A from 15 up to 45; 0 for A under 15. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. A missing or non-finite simulator state scores 0 on that step and restarts both 1 s windows. Success: 1.0 held for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. Closing the hot valve instead, or both, scores 0. In a real trial, per condition: three cameras film the whole run at 30 fps, one straight above each valve's stem axis (600 mm up) and one level with the levers from the +y side, square to the pipes, with a 5 mm grid board behind the valves. Under each stem a printed protractor card lies on the table, centred on the stem axis, with 1 degree marks from 160 to 220 mm radius, labelled 0, 15, 45, 88 and 90. Seen from straight above its axis a lever's centre line keeps its true angle, so A and the hot lever's turn (10 degrees) are read on the cards in every frame, and still is A's change over the last second's 30 frames (2 degrees is about 6 mm at the marks). Frame moved: a mm scale beside the pencil marks at each stub and at the panel (5 mm), every frame. Hands off: in each of the last second's frames the gap from each gripper's fingers to the cold lever and valve is measured on the grid in the overhead and the side view; a view never shows a gap larger than the real one, so 30 mm in either view proves 30 mm in space and the frame passes. Optional, not scored: on a pressurised line the cold stub's open end stops running within 10 s while the hot one runs on.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. Each lever is a hinge on a fixed stem with joint stops at 0 and 90 degrees and 0.20 N m joint friction (est, below a new valve's; read with a spring scale at each reset). Ball, seats, packing and water are not modelled. The model's lever is straight at 97 mm; within 63 mm of the stem the real bar rises to the cut-down stock handle (about 120 mm up). Frame fixed. Surfaces 0.5 / 0.4 (est), pads 1.2 / 1.0.
reset_notes: Turn both levers back to open, along the pipe, pointing at the robot (blue grip on the left stub, red on the right); check with a steel rule that each bar's centre line is still 97 mm up. Check the frame has not shifted against the pencil marks and the stubs are tight in the panel. Before each session, read each valve's turning torque with a torque screwdriver on the stem nut, or a spring scale at the grip's middle (target 0.20 N m, 2.0 N), and record it with the trial; a valve far stiffer than that is worked in on a drained line or replaced.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (demo with one arm idle: left arm alone 1.0, right arm alone 0.0); demo: 1.0
